content.summary_of_the_paper: This article proposes compressibility (in the sense of low Kolmogorov complexity) as a key aspect of the inductive bias of neural networks. In particular, a Kolmogov complexity-based no free lunch theorem is formulated. Moreover, several experiments showing that both realistic datasets and modern neural networks prefer no complexity data are presented.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
At a high level, the main weakness of this article from my point o view is that I had an extremely hard time understanding what was new and why various takeaways/messages were interesting. In part this is because of my lack of background in complexity theory. In part I believe in a variety of places the article could have been improved by additional details:

- In equation (1), what is the role of h_*?
- In section 3.1 and elsewhere: why is it interesting to show that real data is compressible and so doesn’t have large Kolmogorov complexity? Isn’t that pretty obvious? If not, how should one interpret 393.2 MB vs 836.7 MB? 
- The takeaway “As long as a machine learning model fits the data better than random chance, it will form a lossless compression of the labels given a large enough dataset” is, as far as I understand, a completely general fact. Why is it phrased as a takeaway? Is there something novel in the present article about this point? And it is such a generic fact then why is it interesting? 
- The proof of Theorem 1 is almost trivial. Why is it an interesting result? Is this the first time a NFL has been stated in terms of Kolmogorov complexity? 
- It appears that the risk bounds presented in this article are in the regime of fixed model size and increasing dataset size. In that setting I don’t believe that non-vacuous generalization bounds are new or surprising. Perhaps I’m missing the point? It seems significantly more relevant to modern DL to work non-parameterically and allows model and dataset size to grow. In that case, it is not obvious to me which of these bounds will ultimately be non-vacuous. 
- I found the takeaway “Takeaway: Language models, both pre-trained and randomly initialized, prefer to generate low-complexity sequences. As a result, we can use even such randomly initialized models to predict the next element in a sequence, as long as the sequence is low-complexity.” Of section 4.3 very confusing. Namely, I think the authors are claiming that a typical sequence predicted by a randomly initialization or pre-trained language model will have low complexity. However, the authors seem to be arguing the converse of this statement: that one can use such models to predict the next token in a low complexity sequence. That seems like a much more ambitious claim.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback regarding clarity of presentation. We address your individual questions below:

“In equation (1), what is the role of h_*?”
h_* denotes a single hypothesis (or parameter vector) which we assign all posterior mass under the point-mass posterior as in Lotfi et al. (2022b).

“In section 3.1 and elsewhere: why is it interesting to show that real data is compressible and so doesn’t have large Kolmogorov complexity?”
Showing that real data distributions tend to exhibit low Kolmogorov complexity is essential for explaining why the no free lunch theorems are violated and why learning is possible in practice.  Namely, if real data distributions did not exhibit this low complexity bias, then learning would not be possible as exemplified by equations 2 and 3.


“The takeaway “As long as a machine learning model fits the data better than random chance, it will form a lossless compression of the labels given a large enough dataset” is, as far as I understand, a completely general fact. Why is it phrased as a takeaway?”
This is a completely general fact, but notable in this context, since the contrapositive shows why learning on high complexity data is impossible: if no lossless compression of the labels is possible, then no machine learning model can fit the data better than random chance given a large enough dataset. However, we have rephrased the takeaway and moved it after section 3.3 to capture the point made in theorem 1.

“Is this the first time a NFL has been stated in terms of Kolmogorov complexity?”
Indeed, to our knowledge, our work is the first to relate the NFL to Kolmogorov complexity formally.  We believe that this NFL theorem helps elucidate the dependence of the NFL on the incompressibility of the data which is not obvious from the other related NFL theorems. We think this result is helpful for understanding why we should not expect the NFL theorem to have any significance for real data, which is highly compressible.

“It appears that the risk bounds presented in this article are in the regime of fixed model size and increasing dataset size. In that setting I don’t believe that non-vacuous generalization bounds are new or surprising. Perhaps I’m missing the point?”
Our work is not concerned with deriving new generalization bounds.  Instead, our work shows that not only can a single neural network model simultaneously achieve non-vacuous compression bounds on a wide range of datasets it wasn’t designed for, but a convolutional neural network that was designed specifically for computer vision can also achieve non-vacuous bounds on a variety of tabular data problems.  These non-vacuous bounds exemplify how the low complexity bias of neural networks is generic, and we do not require domain-specific learners for each domain.

“ I think the authors are claiming that a typical sequence predicted by a randomly initialization or pre-trained language model will have low complexity. However, the authors seem to be arguing the converse of this statement: that one can use such models to predict the next token in a low complexity sequence. That seems like a much more ambitious claim.”

These two statements are actually equivalent.  Consider that the prediction problem asks for $p_\theta(x_n|x_1, x_2, …, x_{n-1})$.  Since $p_\theta(x_n|x_1, x_2, …, x_{n-1}) = p_\theta(x_1, x_2, …, x_{n-1}, x_n)/p(x_1, x_2, …, x_{n-1})$, a model that prefers generating sequences of low complexity will also prefer to predict next sequence elements which form a sequence of low complexity and hence will have higher than random prediction accuracy for low complexity sequences.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors argue that practical neural network models prefer low-complexity data (in the sense of Kolmogorov complexity). They show that common architectures are compressors for labeling functions even in tasks that seem unrelated (e.g., CNNs on tabular data). Also, both pre-trained and random language models prefer to generate low-complexity sequences. Since data in practice have low complexity, the authors argue that the bias of models towards low-complexity data may explain generalization and help model selection. They argue that a single learner which can express complex functions but prefers simple solutions can be used for a wide range of problems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper considers important questions, such as explaining generalization in deep learning and improving model selection. However, I don’t think that the insight in this paper is significant.

Regarding the main theme of explaining the success of deep learning by showing that practical models prefer low Kolmogorov-complexity solutions. I agree that explaining generalization by understanding simplicity bias is a promising direction. The notion of simplicity bias is not new and has been extensively studied in recent years (although not in the context of Kolmogorov complexity). In order to convince that Kolmogorov complexity is the right tool for studying simplicity bias, I think that stronger and more quantitative claims should be shown. Namely, showing that the complexity of practical models is much lower than the complexity of the uniform distribution is a rather weak claim. It is not clear whether such observations are even close to implying any meaningful generalization bound.

Finally, the idea of using a complex architecture but to encourage simplicity (e.g., by using regularization) is clearly not new. This idea is widely used both in practice and in theoretical papers.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The authors make effort to highlight the main ideas, which improves the clarity. However, as I discussed above I think that both the quality of the results and the novelty are not high.
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to the reasons discussed above, I recommend rejection.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment: Thank you for your feedback and for appreciating that our argument that neural networks encode a preference for low Kolmogorov complexity, leading to strong generalization, is in fact novel.  We do want to stress that the preference for low complexity we show in our work both in generalization bounds and in language model experiments is very strong, and moreover it is not clear that we would even desire a stronger simplicity bias than we observe here.  After all, the generalization bounds we compute in Figure 2 (left) are nearly tight in most cases.  The inductive biases of neural networks are especially powerful because while they prefer low-complexity solutions, they simultaneously support high complexity solutions too so that they can solve complex problems and benefit from more data.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies the low-complexity bias of empirically used datasets and neural network architectures, and uses that to explain why no free lunch theorems do not apply to these empirical settings.

Regarding datasets, this paper shows that the labels of various popular datasets have low complexity. Formally they show that for a classification task with C classes, the Kolmogorov complexity of labels of n inputs given the inputs is significantly smaller than n*log(C).

Regarding neural network architectures, the paper shows that:
a) Architecture like CNNs which are usually used for images can be trained to fit tabular datasets and hence compress the labels of these tabular datasets.
b) Both trained and randomly initialized language models assign higher probability to strings of lower complexity.

Finally, the paper also shows that model selection can be automated by trying multiple models and using cross-validation for model selection.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Many of the results in the paper are expected.  For example, the final result about combining a small and big model for having good performance on both CIFAR-10 and Imagenet directly follows from the fact that the smaller model has good performance on CIFAR-10 and the larger one has good performance on Imagenet.

Other results such as those in 3.2, 4.1 ("Neural networks prefer naturally occurring labelings across domains") and 4.3 ("Even randomly initialized language models prefer low complexity") could be interesting if it was shown that other models such as SVMs and HMMs respectively do not have this property. Otherwise, it is not clear why the authors are singling our neural networks in these sections. For example, are the non-vacuous bounds obtained in 4.1 generally true for most machine learning models or is the result specific to neural networks? If they hold for most models then it casts doubt on the claims that these results explain the recent trend of machine learning models to converge to only a few varieties. 

Results in section 4.2 which show that a pretrained GPT-3 assigns exponentially decaying probability to strings as their complexity increases are the most interesting part of the paper. Given the in-context learning capabilities of large language models, we do expect that the probability of string should decrease with its complexity. But the empirical results showing that the decay is (nearly) exponential with complexity are a novel contribution.

Other remarks:
1. The results in Section 4.3 only seem to be significant when complexity is 1, which would correspond to to the either the all 1s or the all 0s string. Is this occurring because randomly initialized models predictions of 1 vs 0 are unbalanced? In particular, how would a model which outputs 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1-p irrespective of the context compare to the randomly initialized model?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written in a clear and understandable way. As described earlier many of the results are expected from earlier works.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I do not find the paper's contributions to be novel. Further their claim in the abstract that "These observations help justify the trend in deep learning of unifying seemingly disparate problems with an increasingly small set of machine learning models." is not well supported as it is not clear if their experiments hold for just deep learning models or most machine learning models in general.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback and for recognizing that our language model experiments are interesting and a novel contribution.  We address your individual comments below:

“The final result about combining a small and big model for having good performance on both CIFAR-10 and Imagenet directly follows from the fact that the smaller model has good performance on CIFAR-10 and the larger one has good performance on Imagenet.”
It is not in general the case that models which perform well on distinct problems can be combined into a single learner which performs well on each of the problems.  Indeed, the No Free Lunch theorem of Shai Ben-David and Shai Shalev-Shwartz precludes this possibility.  Otherwise, we could simply combine learners which perform well on each problem into a single learner which performs well on all problems, defeating the theorem.  Our construction in Section 5 is only possible because a preference for simplicity is effective on real data distributions.  Deploying the simplest model which fits the training data is effective exactly because real datasets tend to prefer simplicity themselves.

“Are the non-vacuous bounds obtained in 4.1 generally true for most machine learning models or is the result specific to neural networks? If they hold for most models then it casts doubt on the claims that these results explain the recent trend of machine learning models to converge to only a few varieties.” The method from [Lotfi et al] for producing generalization bounds that we use in 4.1 is only applicable to neural networks. In particular the high compressibility of neural networks relative to their parameter counts or VC dimension is unusual and not typical for other models. However, we expect that other machine learning models will also share the simplicity bias to different extents. What is especially noteworthy with neural networks is not just their simplicity bias, but rather the fact that this simplicity bias is sufficient to produce generalization even when the network is extremely flexible, and this property is not shared by many other machine learning models. Polynomial regression with enough parameters to fit random labels on cifar-10 will not be able to generalize on the real, structured, cifar-10 dataset and hence it will not be possible to prove corresponding generalization bounds.

“The results in Section 4.3 only seem to be significant when complexity is 1, which would correspond to to the either the all 1s or the all 0s string. Is this occurring because randomly initialized models predictions of 1 vs 0 are unbalanced? In particular, how would a model which outputs 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1-p irrespective of the context compare to the randomly initialized model?”
We point out that the mean generation probabilities are strictly decreasing for the first 4 minimum description lengths, indicating that the randomly initialized GPT models do in fact prefer low complexity sequences.  Also, note that the model described which outputs 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1-p would achieve very poor accuracy on the prediction task of Figure 4 (right) with Minimum Complexity 2 (sequences 01010… and 10101…), whereas the randomly initialized language model achieves 100% accuracy there.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The submission considers several questions surrounding complexity, compression, and no free lunches in machine learning, and reports some results concerning compression of data with neural networks and simplicity biases in large language models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
#### Strengths

1. **Clarity.** The paper is written very straighforwardly and I had no trouble understanding the concepts nor the experimental explorations.

#### Weaknesses

1. The paper does not appear to provide any new insights into the foundational questions that it considers.
For example, whether "the world is a special case of all problems, and thus a No Free Lunch in all generality does not apply," as discussed in the introduction of the submission, was considered explicitly in
[Fernandez-Delgado et al. (2014)](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume15/delgado14a/delgado14a.pdf) and
[Gómez & Rojas (2016)](https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/41826017.pdf) with previous generations of machine learning technologies.
Compression and simplicity via neural network models, as discussed in Section 3 of the submission, were considered as early as [Hinton & van Camp (1993)](https://doi.org/10.1145/168304.168306) and [MacKay (1995)](https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/network.pdf),
and were more recently considered by [Blier & Ollivier (2018)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2018/file/3b712de48137572f3849aabd5666a4e3-Paper.pdf), among many examples.
Simplicity bias and implicit regularization in neural networks, as discussed in Section 4, is already an active area of research, as noted in Appendix A.
The submission does not answer any questions that could contribute to the development of these areas.

3. The explorations in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 do not make sense: The size of a dataset compressed with `bzip2` or a neural network is the description length *under a particular language* (determined by the "compression algorithm"), and not the true (Kolmogorov) complexity as is implied. In other words, the "bound" provided is probably far from tight.

3. Missing discussions of double descent (e.g., [Belkin et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.11118)) and work in overparameterization more broadly, which are closely related to notions of simplicity in deep learning.

Thank you for your review and feedback. To address your questions:

“considered explicitly in Fernandez-Delgado et al. (2014) and Gómez & Rojas (2016) with previous generations of machine learning technologies. Compression and simplicity via neural network models, as discussed in Section 3 of the submission, were considered as early as Hinton & van Camp (1993) and MacKay (1995), and were more recently considered by Blier & Ollivier (2018), among many examples. Simplicity bias and implicit regularization in neural networks, as discussed in Section 4, is already an active area of research, as noted in Appendix A.”

“The size of a dataset compressed with bzip2 or a neural network is the description length under a particular language (determined by the "compression algorithm"), and not the true (Kolmogorov) complexity as is implied.”
Kolmogorov complexity in general only exists with respect to a particular language.  There is no “true” universal Kolmogorov complexity.  Moreover, the difference between Kolmogorov complexities of a single object under two languages is bounded by a constant which does not depend on the object but only on the languages (the length of a program that compiles from one language to the other).  In Section 3, we upper bound the Kolmogorov complexity with respect to Python. The fact that the bound is not tight is irrelevant, having an upper bound is sufficient to show the compressibility of the data and that it is highly unlikely under the uniform assumption, and desire to find the to find the exact Kolmogorov complexity and not just bound it is futile since the value is incomputible in general.

content.title: General Response to Reviewers and AC
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their feedback. While we appreciate the comments, and understand that a number of the reviewers are admittedly not experts in this area, we first want to address several key factual inaccuracies contained in the reviews:

“The final result about combining a small and big model for having good performance on both CIFAR-10 and Imagenet directly follows from the fact that the smaller model has good performance on CIFAR-10 and the larger one has good performance on Imagenet.”
It is not in general the case that models which perform well on distinct problems can be combined into a single learner which performs well on each of the problems.  Indeed, the No Free Lunch theorem of Shai Ben-David and Shai Shalev-Shwartz precludes this possibility.  Otherwise, we could simply combine learners which perform well on each problem into a single learner which performs well on all problems, defeating the theorem.  Our construction in Section 5 is only possible because a preference for simplicity is effective on real data distributions.  Deploying the simplest model which fits the training data is effective exactly because real datasets tend to prefer simplicity themselves.

“I think the authors are claiming that a typical sequence predicted by a randomly initialization or pre-trained language model will have low complexity. However, the authors seem to be arguing the converse of this statement: that one can use such models to predict the next token in a low complexity sequence. That seems like a much more ambitious claim.”
These two statements are actually equivalent.  Consider that the prediction problem asks for $p_\theta(x_n|x_1, x_2, …, x_{n-1})$.  Since $p_\theta(x_n|x_1, x_2, …, x_{n-1}) = p_\theta(x_1, x_2, …, x_{n-1}, x_n)/p(x_1, x_2, …, x_{n-1})$, a model that prefers generating sequences of low complexity will also prefer to predict next sequence elements which form a sequence of low complexity and hence will have higher than random prediction accuracy for low complexity sequences.

“The size of a dataset compressed with bzip2 or a neural network is the description length under a particular language (determined by the "compression algorithm"), and not the true (Kolmogorov) complexity as is implied.”
Kolmogorov complexity in general only exists with respect to a particular language, and in section 3 we upper bound this complexity with respect to python. There is no “true” universal Kolmogorov complexity.  Moreover, the difference between Kolmogorov complexities of a single object under two languages is bounded by a constant which does not depend on the object but only on the languages (the length of a program that compiles from one language to the other).  We have now updated our draft to clarify.

“The results in Section 4.3 only seem to be significant when complexity is 1, which would correspond to to the either the all 1s or the all 0s string. Is this occurring because randomly initialized models predictions of 1 vs 0 are unbalanced? In particular, how would a model which outputs 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1-p irrespective of the context compare to the randomly initialized model?”
We point out that the mean generation probabilities are strictly decreasing for the first 4 minimum description lengths, indicating that the randomly initialized GPT models do in fact prefer low complexity sequences.  Also, note that the model described which outputs 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1-p would achieve very poor accuracy on the prediction task of Figure 4 (right) with Minimum Complexity 2 (sequences 01010… and 10101…), whereas the randomly initialized language achieves 100% accuracy there.

“showing that the complexity of practical models is much lower than the complexity of the uniform distribution is a rather weak claim. It is not clear whether such observations are even close to implying any meaningful generalization bound.”
The point we are making is not about the complexity of practical models being lower than the uniform distribution, but rather about the complexity of the dataset (e.g. labels given inputs) being much lower than uniform, and being able to demonstrate this using the compression scheme induced by a particular model. In fact, as Figure 2 demonstrates, the compressibility of the dataset using the model and the generalization bound achieved by the model are very closely related. Using this compression we are able to prove non vacuous generalization bounds for the model.

content.title: General Response to Reviewers and AC
content.comment:
Aside from these factual inaccuracies, several reviewers suggested that the contributions of our paper are not “novel” or stated that they do not have the expertise to determine what is novel.  We have therefore updated our draft to indicate the novel contributions clearly.  However, we do want to point out that a number of the references included by the reviewers are only very peripherally related. For example, MacKay (1995) connects the marginal likelihood in Bayesian neural networks with minimum description length, arguing that marginal likelihood optimization helps select for simple compressible solutions. Similarly, Hinton & van Camp provide an early example of variational inference, arguing that the variational ELBO, which approximates a marginal likelihood, has a similar effect. While these papers are in some way about compression, they have little to do with Kolmogorov complexity, the no free lunch theorem, whether we can have general inductive biases, whether the same compression approach will work across multiple seemingly unrelated problems, the prior biases of models before training, whether a model in principle can provide good performance in both small and large data regimes, and the other specific content in our paper. Papers about double descent (e.g., Belkin et. al, 2019) are even less related. While we greatly appreciate all of these works, none of the listed papers contain or diminish our contributions. They are complementary.

To reiterate, our contributions are summarized as follows:
We demonstrate the direct connection between compressibility and learnability that is implicit in no free lunch theorems by deriving a new NFL theorem using Kolmogorov complexity.
We show that the low Kolmogorov complexity of real datasets can be directly derived from the machine learning models used to fit them.
We provide strong empirical evidence that neural networks have low complexity biases that are relevant even on data far from what they were designed for.  To this end, we compute generalization bounds using convolutional vision models on tabular data, we showcase GPT-3’s strong preference for sequences generated by shorter expression trees, and we find that even randomly initialized language models have a simplicity bias.
We argue why in principle model selection can be automated into a larger algorithm, and we provide explicit examples demonstrating how multiple models can be subsumed into a single powerful learner, achieving strong performance in different regimes, such as for small and large training sets.

As a more general remark, while papers reasoning about big foundational questions can be hard to evaluate, they are desperately needed by the community. The no free lunch theorem is still regularly used to rationalize the need for inductive biases, which we show is typically not sound. Moreover, it is a commonly held belief that more expressive model classes require more samples to learn, which we demonstrate with several compelling examples is not true. Furthermore, it is still often argued that we need highly tailored inductive biases, which we also show, with several non-trivial examples, is not true. Our paper is not the only paper concerned with these questions, but all of the specific contributions enumerated in the bullets above are novel, and help contribute complementary and valuable perspectives to fundamental discussions about generalization.
